obtained.how: the publisher's typeset PDF as posted in the SEDAR (SouthEast Data, Assessment and Review, NOAA Fisheries/fishery management councils) public document library, reference document SEDAR12-RD13

bibliography.note: The article runs 627–647 (its last reference page is printed 647), as the paper has; Crossref's 627–642 is Crossref's error. PDF p. N = journal p. 626 + N.

claims.claim: body size gives natural mortality of 1.9 yr⁻¹ at 10 cm, falling to 0.50 at 43 cm, for chain pickerel (Lorenzen 1996; project calculations)
claims.location: p. 627 (PDF p. 1), Abstract; p. 632 (PDF p. 6), Table I ('Natural' row)
claims.quote: a joint mortality– weight relationship for all natural ecosystems was estimated with parameters
claims.conditions: M = Mu·W^b with Mu = 3.00 yr⁻¹ (90 % CL 2.70–3.30) at 1 g wet weight and b = −0.288 (−0.315 to −0.261); 308 data from lakes, rivers and the ocean; juveniles and adults (data explicitly on eggs or larvae excluded); total natural mortality
claims.note: Working, with the project's chain pickerel Ws (W = 0.002624·L^3.243, from another source, not checked here): 10 cm → 4.59 g → 3.00 × 4.59^−0.288 = 1.93 yr⁻¹; 43 cm → 520 g → 0.495 yr⁻¹. Both round to the paper's figures. Lorenzen's own lake-only fit is Mu 3.37, b −0.291 (Table I), which would give ~2.2 and ~0.55.

claims.conditions: natural ecosystems pooled; the minus signs are lost in the text layer (b = −0.288)
claims.note: W^−0.288 is the source's; L^−0.87 is the project's conversion assuming W ∝ L³ (−0.288 × 3 = −0.86). With a pickerel-like W ∝ L^3.24 it would be −0.93. Lorenzen himself weighted by isometric length (p. 629).

claims.claim: the share of M the lake does not simulate (disease, parasites, birds, mammals, angling) is size-scaled, higher for smaller fish (Lorenzen 1996: M ∝ W^−0.29)
claims.quote: Mortality was modelled as a power function of weight
claims.conditions: total natural mortality in natural ecosystems, b = −0.288
claims.note: Caveat for the rewrite: Lorenzen hypothesises that NON-predation mortality scales more steeply with weight than total natural mortality, as in aquaculture (b ≈ −0.43, p. 627 Abstract), so the predation part must scale less steeply than −0.288. The model applies −0.288 (as −0.87 in length) to the non-simulated causes, which are a mix of predation by unsimulated animals (herons, ospreys, otters) and disease/parasites; the steeper exponent may fit the disease part better.

notes: Also in the paper: within-population exponents for Long Pond (Ontario) pumpkinseed, bluegill, largemouth bass, golden shiner and yellow perch, and a second yellow perch lake (Fig. 3, p. 634), none systematically different from the ecosystem relationship. Lake-only fit: Mu 3.37, b −0.291 (n = 121). Lorenzen (2000, CJFAS 57:2374) later recommends a length exponent of −1, i.e. M ∝ 1/L, a little steeper than the model's −0.87.
